Hi Craig. My name is Nathan. I'm a computer science student who spends too much time on the Mendocino coast, and this spring I went down a rabbit hole reading reviews of your tours. Fifteen years of people describing the same moment: the kayak slides into a cave, the light comes through, and the water glows like a cathedral. Somewhere around the hundredth review I looked at your website, and it didn't look like what those people were describing.

So I rebuilt it. Not a mockup, a complete working site, built from your own photos and your customers' own words. This page walks through what I found, what I changed, and why. Nothing here is a criticism of the business. The business is clearly wonderful. This is about the gap between how good the tours are and how well the internet tells that story.

The short version

  • Your website can't take a booking, and 6 in 10 tour bookings now happen online.1 The new site is booking-ready the moment you say go.
  • Your own facts disagree with each other. The old site says ages 6 and up in one place, 4 and up in another, and lists a tour on the homepage that's missing from the Tours page. Every fact on the new site appears exactly once, correctly.
  • Your best photos were invisible. I recovered 47 full resolution originals sitting on your web host and put the cave light front and center.
  • Your customers already wrote the copy. The new headlines come from their reviews. "The sea carved the cathedral. You paddle in."
  • AI assistants already recommend you first. I tested it. The new site is built to keep that lead as AI search grows.
  • Five pages became thirteen, including pages for the trips people actually plan: families, anniversaries, gifts, whale season, and a straight answer to "will the caves be open?"

What your visitors see

These are untouched screenshots of the current site, taken July 8, 2026.

Small things, but a visitor deciding whether to hand you $320 for a family of four reads them the way you'd read a hand-lettered "watch yur step" sign on a boat. The tours are safe and professional. The website should sound like it.

There are two tours on the current Tours page called nearly the same thing, "Noyo River Nature Tour" and "Noyo Sea Cave Nature Tour," with identical prices and durations, plus a third Noyo listing that is actually a partner's powerboat tour with no note saying so. And the Sunset Glow tour appears only on the homepage. A visitor who goes straight to Tours, which is most of them, never learns it exists.

The same coast, presented like it deserves

Every page was rebuilt this way: one fact, stated once, correctly. Ages 4 and up everywhere. The Sunset Glow tour has a real page. The two Noyo kayak tours became one clear page, and your partner's boat tour is presented proudly as exactly what it is.

What this earns youFewer phone calls asking questions the site should have answered, and more of the calls you want: people ready to book. Trust is the whole product when you're asking a stranger to put their kids in a kayak.

The booking story (the big one)

Here is the thing I most want to show you. This is what it takes to give you money today, versus on the new site.

Booking today

  1. Find the phone number
  2. Call during business hours (from a Bay Area kitchen at 9pm, this means "tomorrow, if I remember")
  3. Hope the date works
  4. Remember to bring payment to the beach

Booking on the new site

  1. Tap "Book a Tour" on any page
  2. Pick the tour, date, and time from a live calendar
  3. Pay. Done. You find out while you sleep.

Your median visitor, and I looked at the county's own tourism research, is a couple around age 60 from the Bay Area, household income around $111,000, planning an overnight trip in advance.2 They book the hotel online, the dinner online, the Skunk Train online. Across the tour industry, about 60 percent of bookings now happen online, and about 2 in 5 of those come from phones.1 Every evening planner who can't book is a coin flip: maybe they call tomorrow, maybe they book the thing they could book tonight.

Here's what I found under the hood, and I mean this kindly: you already own the machine. Your site's code contains a FareHarbor booking button that someone switched off years ago. It's sitting there, commented out, like a boat on a trailer in the yard.

<!-- <script src="https://fareharbor.com/embeds/api/v1/...">
     <a href="...fareharbor.com/embeds/book/kayakmendocino...">BOOK NOW</a> -->

And your FareHarbor account is real and half-configured: two tours are in it, with photos and a working calendar. What's missing is the last mile. Online payments were never switched on (today every date ends with "please call us"), five of your seven tours aren't in the system, and the gift certificate store is empty. None of that is a website problem. It's about 30 minutes in your FareHarbor dashboard, and I wrote up the exact steps to hand you or their support line.

The new site is wired for it either way. Every Book button opens your FareHarbor. Until you flip the switch, the phone number stays front and center on every page, and honestly it should stay prominent forever. A real human answering is a competitive advantage with your customers. The point isn't to replace the phone. It's to stop losing the people who will never call.

One more found dollar: gift certificates. Your coast is where Northern California celebrates anniversaries. The new site has a "Gift a Tour" page ready, phone-based today, one switch away from selling itself while you're on the water.

What this earns youIf online booking captures even a handful of bookings a month that currently evaporate, that's the website paying for itself. This is the single highest-value change in this entire project.

What the machines see

More and more of your customers start their trip by asking an AI assistant instead of Googling. Traffic that AI assistants send to travel sites is up 194 percent in the past year alone.3 ChatGPT has more than 800 million weekly users, and Google now shows AI-written answers to more than 2 billion people a month.4

So I ran the test myself. I asked Claude, one of the big AI assistants, what a real visitor would ask: "I'm planning a trip to Mendocino this summer. Is there anywhere I can go kayaking? Any good tour companies?"

You won. Named first, ahead of everyone. Fifteen years of five star reviews did that, and I want to be straight with you: that lead exists despite the current website, not because of it. Which is exactly why it's worth protecting. Two things on the old site actively work against it:

  • The site's machine-readable business card (called schema) is broken. The part where your hours go literally reads ", , , , , , ". Seven empty commas. The AI isn't playing favorites, it can only work with what it can read.
  • Your site's settings file tells AI systems not to read the site at all. That's a common default someone chose years ago. It didn't matter then. It matters now.

The new site fixes both, and goes further: every page carries complete structured data (business, tours, prices, and a machine-readable FAQ), so when someone asks an AI "how much is the sea cave tour and can my 5 year old come," the answer comes from you, correctly, instead of from a guess.

What this earns youYou're first today. This keeps you first as the way people find tours shifts under everyone's feet, and your competitors haven't noticed yet.

From 5 pages to 13

The old site had five pages, and they were carrying too much and too little at once: one Tours page holding seven products, a homepage holding a tour nobody else could find, and no page at all for the questions people actually plan around. The new site gives every real intent its own front door:

Tours: Sea Cave (the flagship), Noyo River, Sunset Glow, Whale Season · Occasions: Families, Couples & Anniversaries, Groups & Private, Gift a Tour · Practical: Plan Your Trip with the full FAQ, About, Reviews, Contact with a live map.

Nothing was lost. Every fact, policy, and photo from the old site made the trip, minus the contradictions. If you ever move this to your own domain, the old web addresses can be pointed at their new homes so no old link breaks.

Going live, if you want it

Nothing needs to be decided today. The new site is parked at my address, invisible to search engines, costing nothing. If you like it, going live is small and reversible: your domain gets pointed at the new site, your phone number and FareHarbor stay exactly yours, and the old site stays saved. If FareHarbor's online payments get switched on, the Book buttons start working the same hour.

And small changes take me minutes. Different photo, different wording, a tour I got wrong, whatever feedback you have, I'm happy to hear it and quick to make it right. Tell me the caves I mislabeled. I'd genuinely enjoy the correction.
